name: Guevarism
summary: Guevarism is the revolutionary Marxism-Leninism associated with Che Guevara: armed insurrection by a small guerrilla vanguard (the foco) can create the conditions for revolution, especially in the rural periphery. It couples this with proletarian internationalism, hard anti-imperialism, state-led socialist construction, and moral rather than material incentives to forge a selfless 'New Man'.
scope: Guevarism as its defining sources describe it (Cancino, s6; Löwy, s7): the revolutionary Marxism-Leninism of Che Guevara (c. 1959-1967), a current of the 1960s new left built on the foco doctrine, proletarian internationalism, central planning with moral incentives and the new man. Its texts are Guevara's own: the key texts Cancino names (Notes for the Study of the Ideology of the Cuban Revolution, Socialism and Man in Cuba, the Message to the Tricontinental) and his other speeches and essays (Algiers, Guerrilla warfare: A method, the budgetary finance system). Later guerrilla movements in the guevarist tradition (the Zapatistas, the Tupamaros) and Régis Debray's systematisation are other subjects. Guevarism was never a state's official doctrine, so it has no record of its own: Cuba's government practice is Fidelismo's and Cuban Marxism-Leninism's, and Guevara's speeches describing it count only as his words.

market-under-party-rule.rationale: Socialism and Man in Cuba criticises reliance on the law of value and material incentives, and his budgetary finance system favoured central planning over markets.

no-central-bank.rationale: At Punta del Este he praised Cuba's nationalised banking system as its instrument for exercising credit according to the country's needs.

civilians-legitimate-targets.rationale: The Tricontinental message calls for carrying total war to the enemy's homes and places of entertainment, while Löwy points to Guevara's explicit refusal of assassinations and blind terrorism.

technology-never-politically-neutral.rationale: In his budgetary finance essay he says socialist countries can use the imperialist camp's petrochemical technology without fear of catching bourgeois ideology.

avoid-permanent-military-alliances.rationale: In Algiers he called for an alliance of the underdeveloped peoples with the socialist countries and for a great solid bloc against imperialism.

socialism-needs-revolutionary-war.rationale: He holds that in Latin America power will in the main be won by armed struggle, while granting that a peaceful road is theoretically possible.

no-transition-to-communism.rationale: 'Socialism and Man' and his budgetary finance essay both describe a transition period between capitalism and communism, in which commodity relations persist for a time.

physical-labour-duty.rationale: In 'Socialism and Man' he approves that scholarship students do physical work in their vacations and that young people are drawn into work from the outset.

worker-farmer-alliance.rationale: He holds that a peasant army must unite with the working class to take power, and that the guerrilla depends on the peasant and worker masses.

small-step-social-reform.rationale: He told the Youth Congress that a government offering timid agrarian reform cannot call itself revolutionary; reform must transform property relations at once.

workers-anti-imperialist-capitalist-alli.rationale: The Tricontinental message says the national bourgeoisies have lost all capacity to oppose imperialism, and 'Guerrilla Warfare: A Method' rests the struggle on the peasant and worker masses instead.

colonial-socialism-democratic-stage.rationale: The Tricontinental message says there is no alternative to either a socialist revolution or a make-believe one, which Löwy reads as freeing revolutionaries from the dogma of stages.

parliamentary-road-socialism.rationale: He judged a peaceful electoral road theoretically possible but very remote in Latin America, since an elected government starting real change would face the old army.

resist-oppression-despite-death.rationale: The Tricontinental message ends that wherever death may surprise the fighters it will be welcome, so long as the battle cry reaches another receptive ear.

opposition-only-legal-channels.rationale: In 'Guerrilla Warfare: A Method' he says the oligarchic dictatorship must be forced to use violence and that power is won mainly by armed struggle, not only through legal means.

all-land-state-owned.rationale: He told the Youth Congress the agrarian reform gave land to individual peasants who had worked small plots, alongside cooperatives, rather than making all land state property.

abolish-wage-labour.rationale: In 'Socialism and Man' he says people reach their full human condition when they are no longer compelled to sell themselves as a commodity, and wants work freed from that sale.

property-sabotage-justified.rationale: His Instructions to Urban Cadres include sabotage of centres of economic activity among armed actions, and in 1961 he named organised sabotage among the useful forms of struggle in the city.

free-basic-services-for-all.rationale: At Punta del Este he praised making secondary education free and giving the whole people free access to higher education.

armed-resistance-to-occupation.rationale: The Tricontinental message praises the Vietnamese people's armed resistance to US forces and calls for creating many more such fronts.

notes: Second pass (claude-opus-5-5, 2026-11-09) under rules 5. Guevarism has no record (never a state's official doctrine), so every source is words. Answers rest on Guevara's own texts tied to the ideology by the defining sources (Cancino, Löwy) and the local Marxists Internet Archive corpus; Wikipedia only gave leads. First-pass answers deduced from a general value (socialism, materialism, egalitarianism) or from Cuban state practice were nulled with their history kept. Themes searched in the full texts: elections and parliaments, the party and the state, democracy, law and courts, executions, press and art, race, women, religion, health, education, land, banking, money, debt, trade and tariffs, foreign bases, disarmament, the UN and international law, sabotage and civilians. Guevara's published texts say nothing on gender, sexuality, family, religion policy, immigration or the environment, so those statements stay null. In 1961 at Punta del Este he guaranteed Cuba would not export revolution; his mature position (Algiers 1965, Tricontinental 1967) is armed internationalism, and the answers follow it.
